questions.question: Which molecule (A to D) can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light? A H2NCH2COOH, B HOCH2CH2COOH, C ClCH2C(CH3)(Cl)COOH, D H2NC(CH3)2COOH.
questions.answer: C - ClCH2C(CH3)(Cl)COOH (it has a chiral carbon)
steps: Only chiral molecules, which are non-superimposable mirror images, rotate plane-polarised light.
A chiral molecule needs a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
A (glycine) has CH2 with two H atoms, so there is no chiral carbon.
B (HOCH2CH2COOH) has no carbon bonded to four different groups.
D has a central carbon with two identical CH3 groups, so it is achiral.
C has a central carbon bonded to CH3, Cl, CH2Cl and COOH, all different, so it is chiral and optically active.

questions.question: Which of structures A to D is not identical to the other three?
steps: Each structure has one carbon bonded to Cl, OH, CH2CH3 and CH3, so each is chiral and can exist as either of two mirror-image forms (enantiomers).
CIP priorities are Cl > OH > CH2CH3 > CH3. Looking with the CH3 group pointing away, Cl -> OH -> CH2CH3 runs anticlockwise (S) in A, B and C.
A, B and C are therefore the same molecule drawn from different viewpoints.
In D, Cl -> OH -> CH2CH3 runs clockwise (R), so D is the mirror image of the other three. It is the one that is not identical.

questions.question: Which types of stereoisomerism does citronellol (found in rose and geranium oils) show? A optical and geometric, B optical only, C geometric only, D neither.
steps: Citronellol is HOCH2CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH=C(CH3)2.
The CH carrying the CH3 group is bonded to four different groups (H, CH3, CH2CH2OH, CH2CH2CH=C(CH3)2), so it is a chiral centre and the molecule shows optical isomerism.
The terminal alkene carbon is bonded to two identical CH3 groups, so there is no geometric (E/Z) isomerism.

questions.question: How many optical isomers does the molecule shown have? A 2, B 3, C 6, D 8.
steps: The molecule is Br-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(OH)-CH(Cl)-CH3.
Three carbons are each bonded to four different groups: the C-Br carbon, the C-OH carbon and the C-Cl carbon.
Number of optical isomers = 2^n = 2^3 = 8.

questions.question: A single optical isomer of a bromoalkane RBr reacts with OH- by an SN1 mechanism to give a racemic alcohol. Which type of bromoalkane is most likely? A primary only, B secondary only, C tertiary only, D primary, secondary or tertiary.
steps: A racemic product forms when OH- attacks a planar intermediate from either face with equal probability.
SN1 proceeds through a carbocation intermediate, which is planar.
A primary bromoalkane cannot be chiral at the C-Br carbon, since CH2Br has two H atoms, so it cannot be a single optical isomer.
A chiral C-Br carbon needs three different alkyl groups plus Br, which fits a tertiary bromoalkane.
Tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so SN1 is most favoured for tertiary bromoalkanes.
Therefore RBr is most likely a tertiary bromoalkane only.

questions.question: How many chiral centres are there in one molecule of menthol? A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
steps: Menthol is 2-(1-methylethyl)-5-methylcyclohexanol.

Chiral centres are the ring carbon bonded to OH, the ring carbon bonded to the isopropyl group and the ring carbon bonded to the CH3 group. Each has four different groups, since the two ring paths differ.
The CH of the isopropyl group carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral. The CH2 ring carbons and CH3 carbons are not chiral either.

questions.question: A single enantiomer of 2-iodobutane reacts with sodium hydroxide and the product is a mixture of enantiomers. Why? A it is a nucleophilic substitution, B it proceeds via a negatively charged transition state, C it proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, D its rate depends on the concentration of 2-iodobutane.
questions.answer: C - the reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate
steps: Forming a mixture of enantiomers from one enantiomer is racemisation.
Racemisation needs a planar, achiral intermediate that can be attacked from either face.
A carbocation intermediate has a planar sp2 carbon, as in an SN1 mechanism.
OH- attacks the planar carbocation from either side with equal probability.
Equal amounts of two mirror-image products form, giving a racemic mixture.
A is true of all substitutions but does not explain racemisation; B and D do not explain it either.

questions.question: Which pair of compounds can form a racemic mixture when mixed?
steps: A racemic mixture needs two molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other (a pair of enantiomers) in equal amounts.

In A the two structures are different compounds, and the right-hand one has two CH2OH groups, so it is achiral. In C the two compounds are also different, and the right-hand one has two CH3 groups, so it is achiral.
In B both drawings are the same enantiomer, so the mixture would still rotate plane-polarised light.
In D the right-hand structure is the reflection of the left-hand one (H, OH and C2H5 swapped left to right with the same wedge/dash), so they are enantiomers and form a racemic mixture.

questions.question: How many chiral centres are there in a molecule of metoprolol? A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3.
steps: Only the carbon bonded to OH has four different groups (H, OH, CH2-O-aryl and CH2-NH-), so it is the only chiral centre.
The carbon of the isopropyl group bonded to N carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral.
All other carbons are CH2, CH3 or sp2 carbons of the benzene ring, which cannot be chiral.

questions.question: Which pair of molecules, mixed in equimolar quantities, will not rotate the plane of plane-polarised light?
steps: All the molecules are 2-bromobutane (CH3, H, Br, C2H5 on one carbon). An equimolar mixture does not rotate plane-polarised light only if it is a racemate, i.e. a pair of enantiomers.
Assigning R/S (priorities Br > C2H5 > CH3 > H): in A both are R, in C both are R, in D both are S, so each of these pairs is the same enantiomer drawn differently and would still rotate the light.
In B the left structure is R and the right structure is S, so they are mirror images and the 1:1 mixture is racemic.

questions.question: How many chiral centres are in the molecule shown? A 4, B 5, C 6, D 7.
steps: The molecule is a steroid (progesterone). Chiral centres are carbons bonded to four different groups.
The two ring-fusion carbons that carry CH3 groups are chiral (2).
The three ring-fusion CH carbons (two between the B and C rings and the one between the C and D rings) are chiral (3).
The CH carbon bearing the COCH3 side chain on the five-membered ring is chiral (1).
The C=C carbons are sp2, so are not chiral; the C=O carbons and CH2 carbons are not chiral. Total = 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term stereoisomer.
questions.answer: Stereoisomers have the same structural formula (atoms bonded in the same order) but a different arrangement of the atoms in space.
steps: Stereoisomers have the same molecular formula.
They have the same structural formula, so the atoms are bonded in the same order.
They differ only in the spatial (3D) arrangement of their atoms.
Examples are optical isomers (enantiomers) and geometric (E/Z) isomers.

questions.question: Show that the initial rate data for the hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane by hydroxide ions are consistent with an SN2 mechanism.
questions.answer: Rate = k[2-bromobutane][OH-]: first order in each reactant and second order overall, as expected for SN2 (k = 1.2 dm^3 mol^-1 s^-1)
steps: Experiments 1 and 2: [2-bromobutane] doubles (0.150 -> 0.300) with [OH-] constant, and the rate doubles (0.027 -> 0.054), so the reaction is first order in 2-bromobutane.
Experiments 1 and 3: [2-bromobutane] x3 and [OH-] x2 give a rate x6 (0.027 -> 0.162). The x3 is accounted for by 2-bromobutane, so the remaining x2 shows first order in OH-.

Both reactants appear in the rate equation, so both are involved in the rate-determining step: a single bimolecular step, which is the SN2 mechanism. (SN1 would be first order in the halogenoalkane only and independent of [OH-].)

questions.question: A single stereoisomer of 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed. Explain the stereochemistry of the product.
questions.answer: The product is a single enantiomer (optically active, not racemic) with inverted configuration compared with the reactant.
steps: Hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane by OH- follows an SN2 mechanism in one concerted step.
OH- attacks the carbon from the side opposite the C-Br bond (backside attack).
As the C-Br bond breaks, the other three groups flip like an umbrella, giving inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).
Only one enantiomer of the reactant is present, so only one enantiomer of the product forms.
There is no planar intermediate, so no racemisation occurs and the product is optically active.

questions.question: Explain how all the features of the reaction profile for the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane are consistent with an SN1 mechanism.
questions.answer: Two-step profile with an intermediate (carbocation) and a higher first peak (slow, rate-determining C-Br bond breaking), which matches SN1
steps: There are two maxima (two transition states) with a minimum between them, so there are two steps and an intermediate. In SN1 this is the tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C+CH2CH3 formed after Br- leaves.

The first peak is higher, so the first step (heterolytic breaking of the C-Br bond) has the larger activation energy. It is the slow, rate-determining step and involves only the halogenoalkane (unimolecular).
The second peak is lower: the fast attack of OH- on the carbocation has a small activation energy.
Products lie below reactants, so the overall reaction is exothermic.
